title: Broad cycle 22: 48 independently proposed questions
status: Questions only; no product execution, acceptance, performance measurement, or baseline result generated by the author.
conventions: References require independent main-agent mathematical review before first product acceptance.
All 48 cases jointly define this batch; later correction of a demonstrably invalid question must be recorded explicitly, never disguised as a product pass.
Antiderivatives allow additive constants on each connected original domain, unless a globally differentiable primitive is expressly required.
A short expression valid on a stated punctured domain does not authorize filling inherited holes. Domain conditions are part of expected behavior.
Finite derivative means ordinary two-sided derivative unless an endpoint one-sided behavior is separately stated.
Exact-image conversion requires necessary domain/parameter restrictions in addition to a closure equation.
Special-function reference names such as Ei are semantic references with definitions; equivalent supported exact forms are accepted.
Validation inputs are supplemental checks and do not replace full-domain proof. No resource requirement is an observed measurement.

conditions: x real; erf(z)=2/sqrt(pi)*integral_0^z exp(-t^2) dt.

properties: A branch-correct exact named special function is solved; an unchanged integral is unsolved.

proof: The defining derivative of erf is 2*exp(-x^2)/sqrt(pi).
The integrand is entire; the real primitive is differentiable at zero as well as away from zero.
cases.domain: R; one additive constant.
cases.novelty: Gaussian non-elementary primitive; not the previous elliptic or dilogarithmic family.
cases.counterexample: Replacing erf(x) by exp(-x^2) gives the extra factor -2*x.

conditions: x real; nonnegative real sqrt.
proof: Set u=sqrt(x), dx=2*u du, and integrate 2*u*exp(-u) by parts.
The displayed primitive expands as -2+x+O(x^(3/2)) at zero, so its right derivative there is 1.
cases.domain: [0,+infinity); ordinary derivative on (0,+infinity), right derivative at 0.
cases.novelty: Exponential of a radical with a finite endpoint derivative hidden by formal 1/sqrt(x).
cases.counterexample: Replacing the integrand by exp(-sqrt(-x)) changes the real half-line and the chain-rule sign.

conditions: Ordinary real improper integral.
proof: x=sin(t) transforms the integral to J=integral_0^(pi/2) ln(sin(t)) dt.
Reflection gives J=integral ln(cos(t)); adding and using sin(t)*cos(t)=sin(2*t)/2 yields 2*J=J-pi*ln(2)/2.
At zero ln(x) is integrable; near one ln(x)/sqrt(1-x^2)=O(sqrt(1-x)).
cases.domain: 0<x<1; both endpoints improper.
cases.novelty: Logarithmic beta-type endpoint cancellation plus exact trigonometric symmetry; historical log-trig tests were indefinite.
cases.counterexample: ln(x)/(1-x)^2 has a nonintegrable endpoint at one; logarithm vanishing alone does not prove convergence.

conditions: Ordinary improper integral, not absolute convergence or a summability-only value.
proof: Near zero sin(x)/x tends to 1. At infinity integration by parts bounds every tail integral from A to B by 3/A, proving ordinary convergence.
For s>0 differentiate the damped integral with respect to s to get -1/(1+s^2), and use its zero limit as s tends to infinity, obtaining atan(1/s).
The same uniform tail estimate for damped integrals allows s to decrease to zero and yields pi/2; the integral of abs(sin(x))/x diverges by period lower bounds.
cases.domain: x>0; removable integrand limit 1 at zero.
cases.novelty: First explicit Dirichlet conditional-convergence test, with convergence proved before removing damping.
cases.counterexample: integrate(abs(sin(x))/x,x,1,+infinity) diverges to +infinity.

conditions: Ordinary improper integral; do not silently select Cauchy principal value.

properties: Any explicit divergent/undefined diagnostic is accepted; finite 0 is wrong.

proof: The left improper integral is -infinity and the right improper integral is +infinity. They cannot be added to define an ordinary integral.
A symmetric exclusion gives zero, but this is a separate principal-value operation.
cases.domain: [-1,0) union (0,1]; pole splits the integral.
cases.novelty: Interior odd pole distinguishes ordinary divergence from symmetric principal value.
cases.counterexample: Oddness does give zero for an integrable odd function such as x/(1+x^2); it does not resolve this pole.

conditions: a real; ordinary improper integral.
proof: For a>0, (exp(-x)-exp(-a*x))/x=integral_1^a exp(-s*x) ds. Integrating the finite positive-s interval gives integral_1^a ds/s=ln(a), also for reversed limits.
At a=0 the large-x integrand is asymptotic to -1/x; for a<0 its negative exponential term forces divergence to -infinity.
At a=1 the original integrand is identically zero on x>0.
cases.domain: x>0; the origin has finite limiting value a-1 for every fixed a.
cases.novelty: Frullani cancellation of individually divergent origin terms, including the boundary of parameter convergence.
cases.counterexample: Separately integrating exp(-x)/x and exp(-a*x)/x as finite quantities is invalid; ln(abs(a)) is wrong for a<=0.

conditions: a real; x^a=exp(a*ln(x)) for x>0.
proof: x=exp(-u) gives integral_0^infinity u^2*exp(-(a+1)*u) du.
Two integrations by parts give 2/(a+1)^3 when a+1>0. At a=-1 the integrand is u^2; below -1 it grows exponentially.
cases.domain: 0<x<1; only zero can cause divergence.
cases.novelty: Logarithmic Mellin moment with an exact convergence threshold; no analytic-continuation acceptance.
cases.counterexample: At a=-2 the rational formula would be -2, impossible for a nonnegative integrand; the actual integral is +infinity.

conditions: Ordinary real improper integral.
proof: At infinity the integrand is bounded by 2/x^2, so this integral is absolutely convergent.
Integration by parts on [epsilon,R] gives [-(1-cos(x))/x]+integral sin(x)/x; both boundary terms vanish. Apply the separately proved Dirichlet integral.
cases.domain: x>0; removable value 1/2 at zero.
cases.novelty: Oscillatory cancellation in the numerator converts a conditionally convergent integration-by-parts term into an absolutely convergent integral.
cases.counterexample: Changing the numerator to 1+cos(x) produces a nonintegrable 2/x^2 singularity at zero.

conditions: Real square root; ordinary finite integral.
proof: Writing w(x)=sqrt(1-x^2), the sum of the integrands at x and -x is w(x), since 1/(1+exp(x))+1/(1+exp(-x))=1.
The integral is half the area pi/2 of the upper unit semicircle.
cases.domain: [-1,1]; denominator strictly positive.
cases.novelty: Even radical weight with a logistic reflection identity; unlike historical x*sin(x) symmetry.
cases.counterexample: With denominator 2+exp(x), the two reciprocal weights no longer sum to one, so the same result is not justified.

conditions: Ordinary real improper integral.
proof: u=exp(-x) maps the interval monotonically from 1 to 0 with exp(-x) dx=-du.
The integral becomes integral_0^1 sin(u) du. Also the original tail is O(exp(-2*x)), proving absolute convergence.
cases.domain: [0,+infinity); smooth and positive.
cases.novelty: An infinite interval becomes a finite interval under an exponential inner substitution.
cases.counterexample: Omitting exp(-x) leaves a different transformed Jacobian, sin(u)/u.

conditions: x real; ln(x) is real.
proof: Set u=ln(x). The remaining integral is du/u, whose real primitive is ln(abs(u)) on each nonzero component.
Neither x=0 nor x=1 can be filled by the primitive.
cases.domain: (0,1) union (1,+infinity); independent constants on the two components.
cases.novelty: Nested real logarithm with a sign reversal of the inner log and separate domain components.
cases.counterexample: ln(ln(x)) is not a real primitive on 0<x<1.

conditions: x real; Ei denotes the real exponential integral, derivative exp(x)/x on x!=0.

properties: Equivalent exact special-function form with this real branch is accepted. Unchanged integrate is unsolved.

proof: For x<0 one may define Ei(x)=-integral_(-x)^infinity exp(-t)/t dt and differentiate it.
For x>0 define Ei(x)=EulerGamma+ln(x)+sum_(k>=1) x^k/(k*k!); termwise differentiation on compact positive intervals gives exp(x)/x.
The positive-branch definition uses a convergent series to specify the reference, not a requirement that the product expand that series.
cases.domain: (-infinity,0) union (0,+infinity); separate constants.
cases.novelty: Non-elementary exponential-integral primitive with a real logarithmic singularity; distinct from erf, elliptic and dilogarithmic forms.
cases.counterexample: No choice of the primitive makes the ordinary integral across zero finite.

conditions: Real Riemann or Lebesgue integral; finitely many jump points.
proof: The floor values are 0 on [0,1), 1 on [1,2), and 2 on [2,5/2].
The integral is 0*1+1*1+2*(1/2)=2; values at single endpoints do not change it.
cases.domain: [0,5/2]; floor is defined at all endpoints and jumps.
cases.novelty: Integration across discrete jump discontinuities, rather than differentiating a floor-based periodic function.
cases.counterexample: Using x-floor(x) as an antiderivative is wrong: its ordinary derivative is 1 away from integers.

conditions: Ordinary real improper integral split at original hole x=1.
proof: On (0,1), -ln(x)/(1-x^2) is nonnegative; its geometric expansion can be integrated by monotone convergence to sum_(k>=0) 1/(2*k+1)^2=pi^2/8.
Substitution x=1/u shows the integral over (1,infinity) equals the one over (0,1).
The hole at one is bounded, ln(x) is integrable at zero, and ln(x)/x^2 is integrable at infinity.
cases.domain: (0,1) union (1,+infinity); x=1 remains excluded although the limiting integrand is 1/2.
cases.novelty: Inversion symmetry plus a removable interior integrand hole and odd-zeta-series evaluation.
cases.counterexample: Dropping ln(x) leaves 1/(x^2-1), whose ordinary integral across one diverges.

conditions: a and x real; a held constant.
proof: For a!=0 differentiate exp(a*x)*(a*x-1)/a^2 to obtain x*exp(a*x).
At a=0 the original integrand is x, whose primitive is x^2/2. A divergent a-dependent additive constant in the generic primitive must not make the a=0 integrand undefined.
cases.domain: R^2; one additive constant for each fixed a.
cases.novelty: Parameter resonance in an indefinite integration-by-parts primitive, with a vanished denominator requiring a separate branch.
cases.counterexample: Substituting a=0 into the generic quotient gives 0/0 rather than the valid primitive.

conditions: x real; sign(0)=0.
proof: For x>0 differentiate (1-exp(-x^2))/2 to obtain x*exp(-x^2). For x<0 use its negative to obtain -x*exp(-x^2).
At zero the primitive is zero and its difference quotient is (1-exp(-h^2))/(2*abs(h)), which tends to zero.
cases.domain: R; the selected primitive is globally differentiable.
cases.novelty: Stitching two Gaussian-substitution primitives into one global C1 function through an absolute-value zero.
cases.counterexample: -sign(x)*exp(-x^2)/2 has the correct derivative away from zero but jumps at zero, so it is not a primitive on all R.

conditions: x real; ordinary two-sided derivative; sign(0)=0.
proof: Off zero use the product rule on each sign interval.
At zero the original quotient is abs(h)*sin(h)/h, bounded in magnitude by abs(h), hence derivative zero. The displayed expression is defined and zero there.
cases.domain: Original and derivative domains both R.
cases.novelty: A zero of a smooth multiplier removes an absolute-value corner without making the inner factor differentiable.
cases.counterexample: diff(abs(x)*cos(x),x) has no derivative at zero because cos(0)=1.

conditions: x real; minimum is pointwise; ordinary derivative.
proof: The smaller branch determines the derivative on every strict-inequality interval.
Equality occurs exactly at pi/4+k*pi. The two candidate slopes are cos(x) and -sin(x), distinct and nonzero opposites there, so both one-sided slopes differ.
cases.domain: Original domain R; derivative excludes x=pi/4+k*pi for every integer k.
cases.novelty: An infinite periodic family of min-branch crossings, requiring symbolic conditions rather than a finite root list.
cases.counterexample: min(cos(x),-sin(x)) does not differentiate the original min: at x=0 the derivative is 1, while that proposal is 0.

conditions: a>0 real and fixed; x real; real positive-base power away from zero; 0^a=0.
proof: For x!=0 apply the real power chain rule.
At zero the quotient is sign(h)*abs(h)^(a-1). It tends to zero for a>1, has distinct limits -1 and 1 for a=1, and diverges with opposite signs for 0<a<1.
cases.domain: Original domain R. Derivative is all R for a>1; excludes zero for 0<a<=1.
cases.novelty: A continuum of exponents causes a differentiability threshold, rather than coalescing polynomial max contacts.
cases.counterexample: Blindly setting sign(0)=0 in a*abs(x)^(a-1)*sign(x) cannot justify the derivative at a=1 or a=1/2.

conditions: x real; piecewise branches evaluate lazily.
proof: At zero the quotient magnitude is at most exp(-1/h^2)/abs(h), tending to zero.
For nonzero x the product and chain rules give the stated expression.
Choose x_n=1/sqrt(ln(2*pi*n)); then the sine is zero and cosine one, so the derivative is -2/x_n^3 and unbounded as x_n decreases to zero.
cases.domain: Original and first derivative domains both R; derivative is not continuous at zero.
cases.novelty: Flat function values do not imply flat derivatives under a rapidly oscillating inner exponential.
cases.counterexample: Replacing the derivative at zero by undef is wrong; declaring the whole function C1 from its exponentially small envelope is also wrong.

conditions: x,a real; a fixed.
proof: The original left difference quotient at zero equals a. The right quotient is sin(h)/h and tends to 1.
Both branches have value zero at the join, so continuity imposes no extra condition, but differentiability requires a=1.
cases.domain: Original function domain R; derivative at zero exists exactly when a=1.
cases.novelty: Parameter-dependent matching at a fixed piecewise interface, including a valid smooth join.
cases.counterexample: Selecting the branch containing equality and returning cos(0)=1 ignores the left slope when a!=1.

conditions: x real; arg takes values in (-pi,pi]; derivative is of that real function.
proof: For x>0 the argument is atan(x); for x<0 it is pi+atan(x), because x+i*x^2 lies in quadrant II.
Both open branches have derivative 1/(1+x^2), but the original function has no value at zero, so the short derivative formula must retain that inherited exclusion.
cases.domain: R excluding {0}; arg(0) is undefined.
cases.novelty: Differentiation of a complex phase along a real path, with an inherited hole obscured by a regular rational derivative.
cases.counterexample: Extending the rational formula to zero and calling it a derivative of the original arg function fills an undefined point.

conditions: x real; t is a bound integration variable distinct from x.
proof: The fundamental theorem gives derivative exp(-(x^2)^2) with respect to the upper limit.
The chain rule contributes 2*x, including zero; the integral itself is an even smooth function of x.
cases.domain: R.
cases.novelty: Differentiation through a non-elementary integral with a nonlinear moving endpoint and a bound dummy variable.
cases.counterexample: Treating t as a free differentiation variable yields zero and loses the endpoint dependence.

conditions: x real; real sqrt and principal real asin; ordinary two-sided derivative.

properties: Endpoint left derivative at 1 is 0; endpoint right quotient at -1 is +infinity.

proof: In the open interval the derivatives combine to (1-x)/sqrt(1-x^2).
Write x=cos(t) near x=1. The function is pi/2+sin(t)-t=pi/2-t^3/6+O(t^5), and x-1=-t^2/2+O(t^4), so the relative left derivative is 0.
At x=-1+h, both increments contribute sqrt(2*h)+O(h^(3/2)), making the right quotient tend to +infinity. Neither endpoint has an ordinary two-sided derivative.
cases.domain: Original domain [-1,1]; ordinary derivative domain (-1,1).
cases.novelty: Cancellation of two infinite formal endpoint derivatives creates one finite one-sided derivative while the opposite endpoint remains infinite.
cases.counterexample: Substituting into the unsimplified 0/0 formula at x=1 misses the finite left derivative; it still does not create a two-sided derivative.

conditions: x real and nonzero; square roots are principal complex square roots.
proof: For x>0 both roots are positive and their product is 1.
For x<0 both roots are positive imaginary multiples, so their product is -sqrt((-x)*(-1/x))=-1.
cases.domain: R excluding {0}; negative x is permitted in complex evaluation.
cases.novelty: Reciprocal principal radicals fail multiplicativity on the negative axis, despite their radicand product being 1.
cases.counterexample: At x=-1 the original is i*i=-1, not sqrt(1)=1.

conditions: x,y real and x!=y.

properties: A guarded true or the unsimplified equality plus explicit x!=y is accepted; unqualified domain enlargement is not.

proof: Factor x^2-y^2=(x-y)*(x+y) and divide only under the inherited condition x!=y.
At x=y the left side has a zero denominator before evaluation, so the input equality is not an everywhere-defined identity.
cases.domain: R^2 excluding the entire diagonal x=y; this condition must accompany any Boolean true.
cases.novelty: Simplification of an equality must preserve a two-variable excluded locus, not merely a scalar-value identity.
cases.counterexample: The equation is not defined at (x,y)=(2,2); unconditional true would silently erase that hole.

conditions: x,y real.
proof: For real x,y the conjugate quotient is (x-i*y)/(x+i*y). Both denominators are nonzero exactly off the origin.
Multiplication cancels to 1 on this complete punctured plane.
cases.domain: R^2 excluding (0,0); preserve this original exclusion.
cases.novelty: Conjugation of a complex rational unit-modulus map, with a codimension-two inherited hole.
cases.counterexample: For nonreal x,y the conjugation replacements are invalid; with x=i,y=1 the original denominator is zero.

conditions: x real.
proof: Write x=n+u with n integer and 0<=u<1. If u=0 the two floors cancel; otherwise floor(-x)=-n-1.
cases.domain: R; integers are included.
cases.novelty: An integer-lattice condition in simplification, with infinitely many exceptional defined points.
cases.counterexample: The constant -1 fails at every integer, including zero.

conditions: x real; atan principal in (-pi/2,pi/2).
proof: The derivative of atan(sinh(x)) is cosh(x)/(1+sinh(x)^2)=1/cosh(x).
The derivative of 2*atan(exp(x)) is 2*exp(x)/(1+exp(2*x))=1/cosh(x).
The difference is constant on connected R and is zero after adding pi/2 at x=0.
cases.domain: R; all denominators implicit in hyperbolic expressions are positive.
cases.novelty: Hyperbolic-to-circular inverse identity justified globally by derivatives and a normalization, rather than a tangent equality modulo pi.
cases.counterexample: Dropping +pi/2 gives -pi/2 at zero; tangent equality alone would miss this constant branch.

conditions: x real and x!=0 for the complete original difference.

properties: Retain or report the original x!=0 guard.

proof: For every x!=0 both terms are the same.
At zero the subtraction still contains the undefined unguarded quotient; the defined value of the other summand does not make the whole input defined.
cases.domain: R excluding {0}; the right summand is undefined at zero even though the left piecewise summand has a value there.
cases.novelty: A local piecewise hole repair must not be propagated to a separate unguarded occurrence.
cases.counterexample: Returning an unconditional zero fills the hole at x=0.

conditions: x<0 and y<0 real; principal complex square roots.
proof: Let x=-a,y=-b with a,b>0. The square roots are i*sqrt(a),i*sqrt(b), so the cross term is -2*sqrt(a*b).
Subtracting the separately principal 2*sqrt(x*y)=2*sqrt(a*b) leaves -4*sqrt(a*b).
cases.domain: Open negative quadrant; extends continuously to zero boundaries if separately allowed.
cases.novelty: A binomial expansion is algebraically valid while combining two principal radical factors is invalid; negative two-variable sector.
cases.counterexample: For x>0,y>0 the result is instead zero; the negative-sector answer cannot be generalized to all reals.

conditions: x real; nested divisions use their original domains.

properties: Keeping a compact guarded exact expression is acceptable; algebraic identity and inherited exclusions both required.

proof: For T(x)=1/(1-x), T^2(x)=(x-1)/x and T^3(x)=x wherever all three operations exist.
The first three operations exclude exactly x=1 and x=0; for any other real x the three-cycle remains away from both forbidden values. Six cycles give x with precisely these inherited holes.
cases.domain: R excluding {0,1}; all 18 nested operations must be defined.
cases.novelty: Bounded repeated Möbius composition has a short algebraic normal form and a stable excluded set, exposing redundant rebuilding and domain loss.
cases.counterexample: The final x alone is defined at 0 and 1, where the original composition fails. A different map 1/(2-x) does not have period three.

resource_requirements.status: Requested acceptance budgets, not measured observations
requirements: Stop the individual case on the external deadline; record timeout or crash distinctly from mathematically undefined.
No claim about CG50 RAM, SH4 stack safety, or capacity follows from these host requirements.
Record returned expression size; do not expand the input into an unbounded series.

conditions: x,y,t real; t ranges over all finite reals.
proof: Substitution gives t^6=t^6. Conversely any nonzero point has x>0 and t=y/x, with t^2=y^2/x^2=x and t^3=y.
The origin is attained at t=0; it cannot be dropped during division by x.
cases.domain: The full real cusp y^2=x^3, necessarily x>=0.
cases.novelty: Cartesian-to-parametric singular cubic, with a rational inverse away from the cusp.
cases.counterexample: [t^2,t^2] does not lie on the cubic except at special parameter values.

conditions: All variables real; t finite real.
proof: For x!=0 put t=y/x; the equation forces t^2=x+1, recovering both coordinates. For x=0 the equation forces y=0, attained at t=+/-1.
cases.domain: Full nodal cubic; the node (0,0) occurs at both t=1 and t=-1.
cases.novelty: A nodal cubic has two parameter preimages at a singular point; distinct from a cusp and all conics.
cases.counterexample: Restricting t>=0 loses the negative-y branch for x>0.

conditions: t runs over all finite real numbers; exact image required.

properties: An implicit equation with an explicitly retained x>=0 restriction is accepted; closure alone is insufficient.

proof: Every image has x=t^2>=0 and y=x^2. Conversely for each x>=0 choose t=sqrt(x); then y=t^4=x^2.
cases.domain: Closed right half of y=x^2, including origin.
cases.novelty: Polynomial elimination must retain a real inequality, even without rational denominator holes.
cases.counterexample: The algebraic closure equation y=x^2 admits (-1,1), which has no real parameter preimage.

conditions: t real; r>=0; -pi<theta<=pi; exact real image.
proof: cosh(t)^2-sinh(t)^2=1 and cosh(t)>0, so the displayed polar relation is necessary.
Conversely the relation gives x>0 and x^2-y^2=1. Set t=ln(y+sqrt(1+y^2)); then sinh(t)=y and cosh(t)=sqrt(1+y^2)=x.
cases.domain: Right branch of x^2-y^2=1; in principal polar coordinates -pi/4<theta<pi/4.
cases.novelty: A transcendental parametrization of one hyperbola branch, with inverse via a real logarithm and no periodic parameter assumptions.
cases.counterexample: r^2*cos(2*theta)=1 alone includes the left hyperbola branch; theta=pi,r=1 is a counterexample.

conditions: x,y real; r>=0; -pi<theta<=pi.
proof: x*y=r^2*cos(theta)*sin(theta)=r^2*sin(2*theta)/2, proving equivalence without squaring.
The equation implies positive r^2 and nonzero sine. Every admitted polar pair substitutes to x*y=1, and every Cartesian solution has unique r>0 and principal angle.
cases.domain: Nonzero radius; sin(2*theta)>0, giving both hyperbola branches.
cases.novelty: Cartesian hyperbola crossing two disconnected angular sectors without an origin branch.
cases.counterexample: Using r=2/sin(2*theta) forgets the square on radius; at theta=pi/4 the correct radius is sqrt(2).

conditions: Standard radius r>=0; -pi<theta<=pi; theta=pi excluded by the original denominator.
proof: Multiplication by the nonzero denominator gives r+x=2. Squaring r=2-x yields x^2+y^2=(2-x)^2, hence the parabola.
Conversely on the parabola x<=1, so 2-x>0 and r=sqrt(x^2+y^2)=2-x. A point with theta=pi would have y=0,x<0, but y=0 on this parabola forces x=1. Thus no forbidden angle was introduced.
cases.domain: Full real parabola y^2=4*(1-x); implies x<=1.
cases.novelty: Polar conic with a denominator singular angle; sufficiency proof validates a squaring step and all Cartesian points.
cases.counterexample: Squaring a general signed equation r+x=c without proving c-x>=0 can introduce points; this proof relies on this parabola relation.

conditions: Use standard r>=0 and principal -pi<theta<=pi; therefore the returned parameter must satisfy 0<=t<=pi.

properties: The coordinate pair without the necessary parameter interval is incomplete. Signed-radius behavior may be returned only with an explicit distinction from this required standard-radius image.

proof: On the chosen principal angle interval sin(theta/2)>=0 exactly when theta>=0.
Taking t=theta gives the displayed coordinates and proves every admitted polar point is included. The endpoints map directly to origin and (-1,0).
The original r=0 equation permits theta=0, so the origin is included even though a Cartesian point has no intrinsic angle there.
cases.domain: Image of the closed parameter interval [0,pi]; includes (0,0) and (-1,0).
cases.novelty: Half-angle polar relation is not 2*pi-periodic; radius sign and the principal-angle range constrain the returned parameter image.
cases.counterexample: Allowing t=-pi/3 gives (-1/4,sqrt(3)/4). Its standard polar angle is 2*pi/3 and radius 1/2, while the required sin(theta/2) is sqrt(3)/2; hence this point is outside the stipulated image. Allowing t beyond pi also changes the specified relation domain.

conditions: a,x,y,t real; t finite real; a fixed.
proof: For a>0 the two nonnegative terms can sum to zero only at the origin.
For a=0 the equation is y^2=0, leaving x unrestricted. For a<0 factor y^2-(-a)*x^2 and obtain y=+/-sqrt(-a)*x.
In every case the listed parameters attain every permitted Cartesian point, including origin.
cases.domain: a>0 singleton; a=0 line; a<0 union of two real lines.
cases.novelty: A parameter changes the real conic dimension and number of components; requires classification before dividing by a or taking real sqrt(a).
cases.counterexample: Returning just the origin at a=0 loses every nonzero point on y=0; keeping two imaginary lines for a>0 misstates the real image.

conditions: Real two-sided limit.
proof: Taylor theorem with remainder gives sin(x)=x-x^3/6+O(x^5). Divide the difference by x^3.
cases.domain: Original quotient defined for x!=0 near zero.
cases.novelty: Third-order cancellation in an elementary limit, distinct from historical logarithmic endpoint rules.
cases.counterexample: Directly substituting zero gives 0/0, not zero; replacing x^3 by x^2 changes the limit to zero.

conditions: x real; 1+x>0 and x!=0; real power via ln(1+x).
proof: ln(1+x)/x=1-x/2+O(x^2). Exponentiating gives (1+x)^(1/x)=exp(1)*(1-x/2+O(x^2)).
Subtract and divide by x; both admissible sides have the same limit.
cases.domain: (-1,0) union (0,+infinity).
cases.novelty: First correction of a variable-base variable-exponent indeterminate power, rather than differentiating it only off zero.
cases.counterexample: Replacing the inner expression by its leading limit exp(1) before forming the quotient incorrectly produces zero.

conditions: n is an integer >=0; finite sum.
proof: The coefficient of z^n in (1+z)^n*(1+z)^n is sum binomial(n,k)*binomial(n,n-k).
Use binomial symmetry and (1+z)^(2*n) to obtain the stated coefficient.
cases.domain: All such n, including the one-term n=0 sum.
cases.novelty: Finite combinatorial convolution with symbolic upper limit, rather than old finite-difference or rational-binomial sums.
cases.counterexample: sum(binomial(n,k),k,0,n) is 2^n, not binomial(2*n,n).

conditions: n is an integer >=0; matrix power, not entrywise power.
proof: Write A=I+N with N^3=0. The finite binomial theorem for commuting I,N leaves I+n*N+n*(n-1)*N^2/2.
Nilpotence makes this identity exact; diagonalizability is not required.
cases.domain: All nonnegative integer n, including n=0.
cases.novelty: Symbolic powers of a non-diagonalizable Jordan block, including the second superdiagonal.
cases.counterexample: At n=2 the (1,3) entry is 1, so keeping only I+n*N is wrong.

conditions: n is an integer >=0; n=0 uses the empty-product convention 1.
proof: The even product is 2^n*n!, the odd product through 2*n-1 is (2*n)!/(2^n*n!), and through 2*n+1 is (2*n+1)!/(2^n*n!).
Taking the square of the even product and dividing by both odd products gives the stated formula. It also gives 1 at n=0.
cases.domain: All nonnegative integer n; no product denominator vanishes.
cases.novelty: Finite Wallis product normalized by exact factorial ratios, not floating-point multiplication or a geometric product.
cases.counterexample: Its infinite limit pi/2 is not the value for finite n; n=1 gives 4/3.

conditions: a real or complex; exact symbolic matrix inverse.
proof: Multiply the two displayed matrices in both orders; each product is the 2 by 2 identity.
The determinant is -1 independent of a, so a=0 is regular even though a pivot-first elimination may try to divide by a.
cases.domain: All a; determinant is identically -1.
cases.novelty: A symbolic pivot can vanish although the full matrix stays invertible; demands an answer valid on the entire parameter domain.
cases.counterexample: The rule requiring a!=0 loses the valid inverse at a=0.

conditions: Exact integer arithmetic; nonnegative Euclidean remainder (positive modulus).
proof: Repeated squaring with reduction modulo 1009 computes the reference exactly; the proof certificate is the residues of 2^(2^j), j=0,...,9.
These residues are [2, 4, 16, 256, 960, 383, 384, 142, 993, 256]. Since 1000=512+256+128+64+32+8, multiply the corresponding six residues and reduce modulo 1009.
cases.domain: Finite integers only; no floating-point approximation.
cases.novelty: Large exact integer followed by modular reduction, with a short independently reproducible certificate.
cases.counterexample: Converting 2^1000 to a decimal floating approximation before taking a remainder cannot certify the exact answer.

conditions: Exact 6 by 6 rational Hilbert matrix; no float conversion.
proof: Cauchy determinant identity for H_ij=1/(i+j+1), i,j=0,...,5, gives product_(i<j)(j-i)^2 / product_(i,j)(i+j+1).
Equivalently this is (product_(j=0)^5 j!)^4 / product_(j=0)^11 j!, reducing to the displayed exact rational.
Positive definiteness also follows from v^T*H*v=integral_0^1 (sum_(j=0)^5 v_j*x^j)^2 dx>0 for nonzero real v.
cases.domain: Finite fixed input with 36 entries; nonsingular positive definite matrix.
cases.novelty: Bounded dense rational determinant with very small exact result; complements earlier symbolic rank-one determinant without reusing its structure.
cases.counterexample: A numerically tiny determinant is not an exact zero and does not establish singularity.
